title: Teaching on Purpose #15: Continuous and Enhanced Provision
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: In this installment of his 'Teaching on Purpose' series, Kohlbeck interviews early-years teacher Sophie Darling to explain continuous and enhanced provision as deliberate mechanisms for practice, consolidation and feedback rather than as unstructured play. He argues continuous provision -- the stable, carefully planned resources available to children throughout the day -- functions as an extension of explicit teaching, giving children the repeated encounters with taught content that durable learning requires. Enhanced provision then temporarily layers in new resources or prompts tied to what has just been taught, correcting a common misreading of it as merely a themed or novelty activity. Kohlbeck also connects the approach to adaptation, arguing that varying the representational tools available (verbal, constructive, drawn, symbolic) lets different children demonstrate the same underlying concept without being held back by confidence, language, or fine-motor limitations. A worked example -- comparing quantities with 'more than/fewer than/the same as' language -- shows how a single enhanced-provision area can support five different modes of demonstrating the same conceptual understanding.
points: Kohlbeck argues continuous provision is best understood through the lens of practice rather than play, since durable learning depends on repeated, self-directed encounters with taught content rather than a single explanation.

Enhanced provision is distinguished from continuous provision by being temporary and tightly tied to what was just explicitly taught, correcting the common mistake of treating it as a themed or novelty activity.

The piece frames enhanced provision as an equity tool for adaptation: varying representational modes (verbal, physical, drawn, symbolic) lets children demonstrate the same concept despite differences in confidence, language, or fine-motor skill.

A worked classroom example shows one enhanced-provision maths area (balance scales, sentence stems, sorting trays) supporting five distinct but equivalent ways for children to show they understand comparing quantities.
quotes: Continuous provision refers to the carefully planned resources, materials and experiences that remain available for children to access independently throughout the day. Rather than rotating activities or relying solely on adult-directed tasks, practitioners organise the environment so that children repeatedly encounter opportunities to explore, apply and revisit important knowledge and skills.

In this sense, continuous provision is not separate from teaching but an extension of it. It is the bridge between explicit instruction and secure learning, providing the repetition, consolidation and feedback that durable learning depends upon.

The distinction is important because enhanced provision is often mistaken for a themed activity or an invitation to play. Whilst it may be engaging, its educational purpose should be much more precise.

By thoughtfully enhancing an area with different resources or representational tools, practitioners can provide multiple routes to the same learning goal. One child may explain an idea verbally, another may construct it, another may draw it and another may represent it using physical objects.
Each child is demonstrating the same conceptual understanding (comparing quantities) but through a different mode of expression.
